analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance program covering every U.S. resident with no deductibles or copays, funded by new taxes.
analysis.headline: A universal, single-payer health care bill with 59 House cosponsors was referred to five committees, sent to subcommittees, and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee coverage, military health coverage, and employer insurance with a universal public program run by the states under federal rules. Every U.S. resident would get comprehensive coverage — hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, and long-term care — with no deductibles or copayments for most care. It would be funded by an 8.7% payroll tax on employers, a 2.2% income tax on individuals, and higher tobacco taxes. Private insurance that duplicates the public benefits would be banned.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident — the roughly 40 million then uninsured, people denied coverage for pre-existing conditions, and anyone facing deductibles, copays, or losing employer insurance — would be enrolled automatically and covered for life, with benefits that travel between states. Patients could keep any willing provider, and providers could not bill patients beyond the program payment. Doctors and hospitals would get a guaranteed payer for every patient instead of uncompensated care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. resident, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien would be automatically entitled to comprehensive health benefits under a state-administered program, effective January 1, 1997 [S2] [S3].

No deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments could be charged for acute care or preventive services; nursing facility and home long-term care carry coinsurance reduced or waived for people near the poverty line [S2] [S3].

Covered benefits include hospital care, physician services, prescription drugs, dental, mental health and substance abuse treatment, home and community-based long-term care, hospice, and preventive services [S2] [S3].
Benefits are portable between states, with waiting periods capped at three months, and providers must accept program payment as payment in full — no balance billing of patients [S2] [S3].
The bill would have superseded Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and CHAMPUS, folding their funding into a single American Health Security Trust Fund [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new 8.7% excise tax on wages, individuals a 2.2% tax on taxable income, and smokers higher tobacco excise taxes. Health insurers would lose the market for coverage duplicating the program's benefits, since private insurance duplicating covered services would be prohibited. Drug makers and equipment suppliers would face maximum prices set by a federal standards board, and hospitals would be paid through annual global budgets rather than per-service billing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, taxpayers, smokers, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The financing is a large new tax burden: an 8.7% employer payroll tax on wages plus a 2.2% income tax on individuals, with no credits allowed against the income tax [S2] [S3].
States must prohibit the sale of any health insurance that duplicates program benefits, so people satisfied with employer or private coverage would lose it and move into the public plan [S2] [S3].

Hospitals would be paid through annual global budgets rather than for each service, and a national health security budget capped at GDP growth would constrain total health spending — supporters call this cost control; critics of such systems argue it can mean waiting or rationing [S2] [S3].
Long-term care carries significant cost-sharing — 35% coinsurance for nursing facility services and 20% for home and community-based care — for all but the lowest-income enrollees [S3].

A federal standards board would set approved-drug lists, maximum prices, and practice guidelines that limit coverage of services outside them, concentrating major coverage decisions in a single national body [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered the largest possible expansion of public health security — universal coverage, no cost-sharing for acute care, and an end to medical debt and insurer denials — paid for with broad taxes that in most cases would replace premiums and out-of-pocket costs people already pay. The honest trade-offs are real: it abolished private coverage many people were satisfied with, imposed heavy transition and budgeting demands on states, and gave an unelected national board sweeping power over prices and covered services. It was a maximal single-payer proposal with no phase-ins or opt-outs, which made it politically easy to attack and easy to bury.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in March 1995 and referred to five House committees, it was sent to four subcommittees that spring and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 with it still sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the American Health Security Act of 1995 on March 9, 1995, joined by 55 other House members as original cosponsors [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred to the Commerce Committee and, in addition, to Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, National Security, and Veterans' Affairs [S1] [S5].

Between March 16 and April 5, 1995, it was referred to subcommittees on Health, Human Resources and Intergovernmental Relations, Military Personnel, Health and Environment, and Hospitals and Health Care [S5].
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred; the last recorded action is the April 5, 1995 subcommittee referral [S1] [S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and other parts of the private health care industry kept the existing employer-based system, since the bill that would have replaced private coverage and set drug price caps never advanced. Employers and smokers were spared the new taxes, and the uninsured and underinsured remained without coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug makers, and the status quo

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as principal sponsor.

for.name: 56 House Democrats and 2 Independents
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Waxman, Conyers, Stark, Pelosi, and Sanders

against.name: 104th House Republican majority
against.role: House majority controlling the committee and floor agenda
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before any committee for a vote or scheduled it on the floor during the two years it was in their hands.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers whose core business the bill would have replaced
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer proposals of this era, which would have banned duplicative private coverage and made the government the payer for nearly all care.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Drug makers facing a federal board with power to set maximum prices
against.what_they_did: Opposed national drug price controls and single-payer proposals throughout the 1990s health care debates.

sides.party_line_note: All 59 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; the bill was referred to committees controlled by the new Republican House majority in March 1995 and no action ever followed, so the partisan split is visible in sponsorship and in whose agenda the bill died on rather than in any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have superseded employer, Medicare, Medicaid, and federal-employee coverage and banned the sale of any private insurance duplicating program benefits, eliminating insurers' core market. Their gain from the bill's death was the public's continued exposure to premiums, deductibles, and coverage denials.

A federal board would have created an approved-drug list and set maximum prices, ending the ability to charge unchecked prices. The bill's failure preserved unrestricted U.S. drug pricing, which consumers pay for at the pharmacy.

Hospitals would have gained a payer for every patient, ending uncompensated care, but would have lost per-service billing to annual global budgets under a national spending cap. The current system keeps both the bad debt and the fee-for-service revenue.
The bill raised excise taxes on tobacco products to help finance coverage, a cost that falls on the industry and its customers.

Employers would owe a new 8.7% payroll tax, but many would stop paying health premiums that often exceed that cost, and the bill let employers keep offering extra benefits. Employers that already offered coverage bore the burden of the transition either way.
